tagline: SNCC co-founder, Georgia legislator, first SPLC president, and NAACP board chairman
burial: Julian Bond is memorialized at South-View. Find a Grave lists a South-View plot (Section E4, Block 1NS-E-335-B), and Henderson's South-View book (2018) includes him. However, NPR/WVTF reported that his family scattered his ashes over the Gulf of Mexico in August 2015, and no source we found explains what is physically at South-View.

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Horace Julian Bond was born on January 14, 1940, in Nashville, Tennessee. His father, Horace Mann Bond, was the first president of Fort Valley State College (1939) and the first African American president of Lincoln University in Pennsylvania (1945). His mother, Julia (Washington) Bond, was a librarian. Julian Bond married Alice Clopton on July 28, 1961; they divorced on November 10, 1989. Their children were Phyllis Jane, Horace Mann II, Michael Julian, Jeffery (spelled Jeffrey Alvin by CNN), and Julia Louise. CNN also lists a daughter, Mia, with Deborah Kaye Moore. On March 17, 1990, Bond married Pamela Sue Horowitz, a lawyer at the Southern Poverty Law Center, and they remained married until his death.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Julian Bond entered Morehouse College in Atlanta in 1957. At Morehouse he swam on the varsity swim team, helped found the literary magazine The Pegasus, and interned at Time magazine. He left Morehouse in 1961 to work in the civil rights movement, later returned, and earned a B.A. in English in 1971. Over his lifetime Julian Bond received 21 honorary degrees, and from 1992 to 2012 he himself taught civil rights history at the University of Virginia.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Julian Bond was elected to the Georgia House of Representatives in 1965, but the House refused to seat him because he endorsed a SNCC statement opposing the Vietnam War. In December 1966 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the exclusion unconstitutional, and Bond was sworn in on January 9, 1967. He served in the House until 1974 and then in the Georgia Senate (1975–1986, according to CNN), where he was the first African American chair of the Fulton County Senate delegation and chaired the Consumer Affairs Committee. In 1986 he gave up his Senate seat to run for Congress and lost to his longtime friend John Lewis. Bond was the first president of the Southern Poverty Law Center (1971–1979) and stayed on its board for life. He was president of the NAACP Atlanta branch from 1974 to 1989 and chairman of the NAACP board from 1998, succeeding Myrlie Evers-Williams. He hosted America's Black Forum (1980–1997), taught civil rights history at the University of Virginia (1992–2012), was a visiting professor at American University, and wrote for the Nation, Life, and the New York Times.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: Julian Bond helped organize the Committee on Appeal for Human Rights at Morehouse in 1960, whose nonviolent protests helped integrate Atlanta theaters, lunch counters, and parks. In March 1960 he was arrested at a sit-in at the segregated Atlanta City Hall cafeteria. At Easter 1960 he helped form the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) in Raleigh, North Carolina, becoming its communications director and editor of the Student Voice. In 1961 he left Morehouse to work on the protest newspaper the Atlanta Inquirer. At the 1968 Democratic National Convention he helped a challenge delegation from Georgia unseat the regular Democrats. In 1971 he led a widely publicized voter registration drive in heavily Black areas of Georgia. Bond chaired the Southern Election Fund, which aided candidates in 11 Southern states, and on April 2, 1985, he was arrested at an anti-apartheid protest outside the South African Embassy.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Julian Bond died on August 15, 2015, at age 75, while vacationing in Fort Walton Beach, Florida. The Catholic News Service obituary, citing his wife Pamela Horowitz, gave the cause as complications from vascular disease. Presidents Obama, Clinton, and Carter offered condolences. About 1,200 people attended a memorial at the Lincoln Theatre in Washington, D.C., and at the SPLC's Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery, Alabama, mourners spread rose petals on the reflecting pool. Bond narrated the SPLC's Oscar-winning documentary A Time for Justice and the Oscar-nominated Shadow of Hate. He received the National Freedom Award in 2002 and 21 honorary degrees.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Julian Bond was the first African American to have his name placed in nomination for U.S. vice president, at the 1968 Democratic National Convention; he withdrew because at 28 he was below the constitutional minimum age of 35. Bond hosted Saturday Night Live on April 9, 1977. He was the Southern Poverty Law Center's first president. After his death in 2015, his family scattered his ashes over the Gulf of Mexico, according to NPR.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Julian Bond's birth date is January 14, 1940, per the New Georgia Encyclopedia and CNN; a Catholic News Service obituary says January 15. His death date is August 15, 2015, per NGE and CNN; the CNS text says August 16 in "Walton Beach," though its own photo caption says August 15. Find a Grave gives his first election to the Georgia House as 1966, while NGE and CNS say 1965. CNN dates his SNCC communications director role to 1961–1966. For the Georgia Senate, CNN gives 1975–1986, NGE says he was elected in 1974 but calls the tenure "about twenty years," and CNS says "a dozen" years. His NAACP chairmanship ended in 2010 per CNN and Find a Grave, consistent with SPLC's "12 years"; CNS says 2009. On burial, Find a Grave lists a South-View plot, but NPR/WVTF reported his ashes were scattered over the Gulf of Mexico, and the 2016 Georgia Historical Society South-View marker does not name him.

tagline: First Black woman in the Georgia General Assembly and architect of Atlanta's 1973 City Charter
burial: Grace Towns Hamilton is listed as buried at South-View in Henderson's South-View book (2018), and Wikipedia, citing Notable American Women (2005), says the same. We found no Find a Grave memorial, cemetery record or obituary confirming it, and the 2016 Georgia Historical Society marker at the cemetery does not name her.

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Grace Towns Hamilton was born on February 10, 1907, in Atlanta, the oldest of four surviving children of Harriet McNair and George Alexander Towns, a professor of English and pedagogy at Atlanta University. In 1930 she married Henry Cooke Hamilton, son of Atlanta builder Alexander D. Hamilton. Their only child, Eleanor, was born in 1931 in Memphis. A Kiddle mirror of the South-View Cemetery article lists her father, George Alexander Towns, among South-View's notable burials, which makes a family plot plausible but unconfirmed.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Grace Towns Hamilton earned her undergraduate degree from Atlanta University in 1927 and an M.A. in psychology from Ohio State University in 1929. From 1927 to 1930 she taught psychology at Clark College and the Atlanta School of Social Work, and in Memphis during the 1930s she taught psychology at LeMoyne College. Her father, George Alexander Towns, was himself a professor of English and pedagogy at Atlanta University, the school where she earned her first degree.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Grace Towns Hamilton spent 1930 to 1941 in Memphis, where she taught at LeMoyne College, surveyed Black workers for the WPA, and developed interracial YWCA college programs. She returned to Atlanta in 1941 and in 1943 became executive director of the Atlanta Urban League, among the earliest women in such a post, pushing for education, health care, housing, and voting rights. She lost the post in 1961 after conflict with the National Urban League. In a June 1965 special election she was one of eight African Americans elected to the Georgia House of Representatives, the lower house of the General Assembly, becoming the first Black woman elected to the Georgia General Assembly; she was sworn in in January 1966. The research notes describe her service only in the House, not the Georgia Senate. She was the principal architect of the 1973 Atlanta City Charter, which made Black representation on the City Council proportional to population. She lost her reelection bid to Mable Thomas in September 1984, and her term ended in January 1985. From January 1985 to January 1987 she advised the U.S. Civil Rights Commission.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: Grace Towns Hamilton's 1965 election made her part of the first group of Black members of the Georgia House of Representatives since Reconstruction. In 1964 Mayor Ivan Allen Jr. appointed her to Atlanta's Fund Appeals Board, and in 1966 President Lyndon Johnson appointed her to the Committee on Recreation and Natural Beauty. Andrew Young credited Hamilton with making possible his 1972 election as the first Black congressman from Atlanta's Fifth District; Georgia Women of Achievement adds that he was the first Black Georgian elected to Congress since 1870. In the reapportionment fight after the 1980 census, Hamilton sided with white leadership over the shape of the Fifth District, a stance that angered many in Atlanta's Black community.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Grace Towns Hamilton died on June 17, 1992. The Atlanta Journal ran a front-page obituary calling her a "great leader and public servant." She was inducted into Georgia Women of Achievement in 2006. The Georgia Legislative Black Caucus's Grace Towns Hamilton Leadership Award is named for her, as is Grady Memorial Hospital's Women's and Infants' Pavilion. Her papers are held at the Robert W. Woodruff Library of the Atlanta University Center, and a biography, Grace Towns Hamilton and the Politics of Southern Change by Lorraine Nelson Spritzer and Jean B. Bergmark, was published by the University of Georgia Press.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Grace Towns Hamilton was the first African American woman in the Deep South elected to a state legislature, according to UGA Press. She was the principal architect of Atlanta's 1973 City Charter. She led the Atlanta Urban League from 1943 to 1961. Andrew Young credited her with making his 1972 election to Congress possible. Grady Memorial Hospital's Women's and Infants' Pavilion bears her name.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Henderson's South-View book (2018) says Grace Towns Hamilton served in the Georgia Senate, but the New Georgia Encyclopedia says her 1965 election made her one of the first Black members of the lower house, the Georgia House of Representatives, since Reconstruction. Sources differ on when Grace Towns Hamilton's legislative service ended. The New Georgia Encyclopedia gives 1965–1985 and calls it "eighteen years"; Wikipedia gives her term as ending January 14, 1985; and a search summary (not directly verified) attributed 1965–1984 to UGA Press. She lost her reelection bid in September 1984, so the 1984 and 1985 dates may reflect the election and the end of her term. Her burial is also uncertain: Wikipedia and a Kiddle mirror place her at South-View Cemetery, but the 2016 Georgia Historical Society South-View marker does not name her and no cemetery record was found.

tagline: AME bishop, Civil War chaplain, Reconstruction legislator, and advocate of emigration to Africa
burial: Henry McNeal Turner is buried at South-View Cemetery: the Georgia Historical Society's 2016 South-View marker names him among the cemetery's notable burials, and Find a Grave memorial #14775222 places him there (the New Georgia Encyclopedia says only that he was buried in Atlanta).

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Henry McNeal Turner was born free in 1834 at Newberry Courthouse, South Carolina, according to the New Georgia Encyclopedia; Find a Grave and Mother Bethel AME give the date as February 1, 1834. He was never enslaved. His parents were Sarah Greer and Hardy Turner. His paternal grandmother was a white plantation owner, and family legend says his maternal grandfather, David Greer, arrived on a slave ship. Turner married four times: Eliza Peacher (married 1856, died 1889), daughter of a wealthy Black builder in Columbia, South Carolina, with whom he had 14 children, four of whom survived to adulthood; Martha Elizabeth DeWitt (1893); Harriet A. Wayman (1900); and Laura Pearl Lemon (1907).

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Henry McNeal Turner had no formal degrees described by the New Georgia Encyclopedia. Around age 15 he worked as a janitor at a law firm in Abbeville, South Carolina, and the lawyers there helped educate him. He was licensed to preach in 1853 and learned much of his craft as an itinerant evangelist traveling across the South, preaching in Macon, Athens, Atlanta, and New Orleans before joining the AME Church in St. Louis in 1858.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Henry McNeal Turner was licensed to preach in 1853 and worked as an itinerant evangelist in Macon, Athens, Atlanta, New Orleans, and elsewhere. In 1858 he moved to St. Louis and joined the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church, later holding pastorates in Baltimore and Washington, D.C., where he befriended Charles Sumner and Thaddeus Stevens. In 1863 he helped organize the 1st Regiment, U.S. Colored Troops, in his churchyard and was mustered in as its chaplain, and he is widely recognized as the first Black chaplain in the U.S. Army. In 1865 he resigned a reassigned chaplaincy in Atlanta and began organizing AME churches across Georgia. He became manager of the AME publishing house in 1876, and in 1880 he was elected the 12th bishop of the AME Church, the first Southern bishop elected. In 1885 he became the first AME bishop to ordain a woman, Sarah Ann Hughes, as deacon. He wrote The Genius and Theory of Methodist Polity (1885) and edited The Voice of Missions (1893–1900) and The Voice of the People (1901–1904).

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: Henry McNeal Turner helped organize Georgia's Republican Party, served in the state constitutional convention, and was elected to the Georgia House from Macon, which the New Georgia Encyclopedia dates to 1867. In 1868 the legislature expelled its Black members; Turner spoke against the expulsion without success and afterward received Ku Klux Klan threats. In 1869 President Grant appointed him postmaster of Macon, but he resigned weeks later amid allegations. At Congress's urging he was reseated in 1870, then lost a contested reelection months later, and afterward worked at the Savannah Custom House and pastored St. Philip's AME Church. Turner was a leading advocate of emigration to Africa: in the 1890s he organized the International Migration Society with white Alabama businessmen, and in 1895 and 1896 two ships carried 500 or more emigrants to Liberia, though some later returned. Between 1891 and 1898 he made four trips to Africa, organized AME conferences in Liberia and Sierra Leone, helped merge the AME Church with the Ethiopian Church in South Africa, and sent missionaries to Cuba and Mexico.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Henry McNeal Turner died on May 8, 1915, in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, while traveling on church business, and was buried in Atlanta at South-View Cemetery. His portrait hangs in the Georgia State Capitol. The Georgia Historical Society's South-View Cemetery marker, erected in 2016, names "Bishop Henry McNeal Turner, Reconstruction-era state legislator and African Methodist Episcopal Church organizer" among the cemetery's notable burials, alongside Alonzo Herndon and Rev. and Mrs. Martin Luther King Sr.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Henry McNeal Turner is widely recognized as the first Black chaplain in the U.S. Army, serving the 1st U.S. Colored Troops from 1863. He was expelled from the Georgia legislature with the other Black members in 1868 and reseated in 1870. As the AME Church's 12th bishop, he was the first to ordain a woman as deacon, in 1885. He championed emigration to Liberia, and ships sailed under his International Migration Society in 1895 and 1896. He died in Canada in 1915 and is named on South-View's 2016 state historical marker.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Henry McNeal Turner's birthplace is Newberry Courthouse, South Carolina, per the New Georgia Encyclopedia and Find a Grave (Newberry), but Mother Bethel AME says "near Abbeville, South Carolina"; NGE gives only the year 1834, while Find a Grave and Mother Bethel give February 1. NGE dates his election to the Georgia House to 1867, while Mother Bethel and Find a Grave say 1868. Accounts of how many Black legislators were expelled with him in 1868 are inconsistent: Find a Grave gives both "twenty-five" and "26 other," and Mother Bethel's figures appear garbled, so no number is given here. His role at Morris Brown College in Atlanta is unresolved: Mother Bethel says he served 12 years as chancellor, and Find a Grave says he helped found the college. Mother Bethel also associates him with the declaration "God is a Negro," placing it at "the first Black Baptist convention" with no date; that setting is doubtful for an AME bishop and has not been verified.
